newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Kabila accused of delaying U.N. inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Kabila accused of delaying U.N. inquiry.

text.p: The United Nations said on Sunday the new government in Kinshasa was still blocking a much-delayed inquiry into alleged massacres in the east, where Tutsi-dominated forces are accused of killing Rwandan Hutu refugees.

The new ruler of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Laurent Kabila, had repeatedly promised to cooperate, a U.N. statement in Geneva said, but his government rejected the composition of the U.N. human rights mission and insisted that the inquiry must start from March 1993.
An advance U.N. team, in Kinshasa since June 20 to lay out terms for the investigation, hoped to gain access as soon as possible to alleged massacre sites before a full mission due on July 7.

The supreme United Nations human rights body in Geneva set up the three-member commission in April after the U.N. special human rights investigator for Zaire, Roberto Garreton, called for an investigation into killings in the country's east.
Under its mandate, it should have reported to the U.N. General Assembly in New York by the end of June.
Garreton, an attorney from Chile, angered Kabila by producing a list of 40 sites where his rebels were alleged to have killed people and by saying up to 50,000 people might have died.
He headed a U.N. commission of inquiry in May but his group was refused entry into eastern Zaire by Kabila's former rebels, who are backed by neighbouring Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated rulers.

At the time, Kabila's aides insisted that Garreton must be dropped from the inquiry, that the mission should include local officials and army officers and that backgrounds of forensic experts from Argentina should be vetted.

Kabila's takeover in May of Africa's third largest country after a seven-month bush war has been tainted by reports that his troops systematically killed Rwandan Hutu refugees, including militias who took part in Rwanda's 1994 genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
U.N. and aid officials believe the former rebels are now destroying evidence of killings in areas off-limits to aid workers.

The U.N. statement said the advance team told Kinshasa that it was not authorised to negotiate the mission's composition and mandate. The government had confirmed "the necessity of there being an investigation and continued talks" with the advance team, it said.

The team was seeking official guarantees on the security of the investigators, free access to all areas, protection and preservation of alleged massacre sites and graves, confidentiality of interviews with witnesses and freedom from harassment for all witnesses and others assisting the probe, the statement said.
